topic: describing composition of transformations and symmetry
subtitle: Carrying out a two-step composition of rigid motions, naming the single transformation that does the same job, and describing the line and rotational symmetry of a figure

traps.desc: gave the distance between the two mirror lines instead of the distance the point travelled, which is twice as far

problems.desc: Open description, part (c). The student must name the single transformation equivalent to reflecting in x = 1 and then in x = 4: a translation of 6 units in the positive x-direction (to the right), with no rotation or reflection. Accept 'translation 6 units right', a vector (6, 0), or an equivalent phrasing, and award full credit only if the answer says BOTH that it is a translation AND how far/which way. Look for the observation that 6 is twice the 3-unit gap between the mirror lines; that is the general result and is worth crediting even if the student states it only for this case.

Open description, part (c). Reflecting in the x-axis and then in the y-axis is the same single transformation as a rotation of 180 degrees about the origin. Accept 'rotation 180 degrees about the origin', 'half turn about the origin', or 'point reflection in the origin'. Full credit requires naming the transformation, the angle (or 'half turn') and the centre. The midpoint result in part (b) is the evidence: the origin sits exactly halfway between every point and its image, which is what a half turn about the origin does.

Open description, part (c). Reflecting in the line y = x and then in the x-axis sends (a, b) to (b, a) and then to (b, -a) — a rotation of 90 degrees CLOCKWISE about the origin. Accept 'rotation 90 degrees clockwise about the origin' or the equivalent 'rotation 270 degrees counterclockwise about the origin'. Full credit requires the transformation, the angle, the direction and the centre. Do not accept 'a rotation about the origin' with no angle, and do not accept 90 degrees counterclockwise, which is the composition taken in the other order.

traps.desc: halved the full turn because the hexagon looks the same after a half turn, missing the smaller angle that also works

problems.desc: Open description, part (c). The student must explain why this parallelogram has rotational symmetry of order 2 (a half turn about the common midpoint of the diagonals maps it onto itself) but no line of symmetry. Accept any answer that uses the shared midpoint found in parts (a) and (b) as the centre of the half turn. For the missing line symmetry, accept any correct reason: the slanted sides lean the same way rather than mirroring each other, so a fold along either diagonal or along a mid-line does not bring the two halves together; or a specific vertex whose reflected position is not a vertex of the figure. Do not accept 'a parallelogram has no line of symmetry' as a bare fact with no reason.

Open justification, part (c). The student must explain why reflecting in two PERPENDICULAR lines always gives the same result as a half turn about their point of intersection. A full answer argues generally rather than only re-checking the given point: reflecting in a vertical line reverses the horizontal displacement from that line and leaves the vertical one alone; reflecting in a horizontal line does the reverse; so after both, BOTH displacements from the intersection point have been reversed, which is exactly what a 180-degree rotation about that point does. Accept a coordinate argument (take the intersection as the origin: (x, y) goes to (-x, y) then to (-x, -y)), or a clear description of the two displacements reversing. Accept the observation that the intersection point is the midpoint of every point and its final image, PROVIDED the student says why that holds for every point and not just this one. Do not accept a check of the single point in part (a) offered as the whole argument.
